items.title: One loop
items.explanation: One loop over n items runs n times. It is O(n), not O(1): count the runs, not the loops you can see.

items.title: Two loops, one after the other
items.explanation: Sequential loops **add**: n + n = 2n. The dominant term is 2n, and dropping the constant gives O(n). Doubling n doubles the count, not quadruples it.

items.title: A loop inside a loop
items.explanation: Nested loops **multiply**: each of the n outer steps runs the whole inner loop, so n × n = n². The count quadruples each time n doubles.

items.title: The triangular loop trap
items.explanation: When i is 0, `range(0)` runs zero times. The inner loop runs 0 + 1 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 times, roughly n²/2. Halving is a constant, so it is still O(n²). Look at the ratios: they head towards ×4.

items.title: Unique pairs
items.explanation: Each pair is checked once: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 0 = n(n − 1)/2. That is the triangular count again, so it is O(n²).

items.title: A fixed inner loop
items.explanation: Nested, but the inner loop is a fixed 5, not n. That gives 5n steps, which is O(n). Nesting only means n² when both loops grow with n.

items.title: Halving each time
items.explanation: i halves every step, so the loop runs as many times as n can be halved before reaching 1: log₂ n. Doubling n adds just **one** step.

items.title: A loop, then nested loops
items.explanation: The two parts run one after the other, so they add: n + n². Keep the dominant term: O(n²). The first loop barely registers by n = 16.

items.title: Three nested loops
items.explanation: Three nested loops over n multiply to n × n × n = n³. Doubling n multiplies the count by 8.

items.title: A halving loop inside a loop
items.explanation: The outer loop runs n times, and each time the inner loop halves j: log n steps. Nested multiplies, so n × log n = O(n log n). This is the shape of efficient sorting.
